_comment: The full CTaDI onboarding form. Section A is asked of everyone. Section B is chosen by the applicant's role. Every question is open-ended on purpose: the LLM scores reasoning and evidence, not keywords. Edit text here and the portal, validation, and scoring prompt all update automatically.
intro: CTaDI brings together people who believe technology should serve people and the planet. There are no trick questions and no right answers — we are looking for how you think, not for keywords. Please answer in your own words.

consent.label: I understand that my answers will be reviewed by the CTaDI team, including with the help of automated tooling, and that a shortlisted application will be read by a human reviewer.

identity._comment: Collected for contacting the applicant and routed to the right question set. These fields are deliberately excluded from scoring.

fields.label: Country or region you are based in
Which role are you applying for?

section_a.title: Section A — How you think
section_a.subtitle: Everyone answers these four. A few honest paragraphs each is plenty.

questions.label: What do you understand by "development"?
questions.hint: There is no textbook answer we are fishing for. Tell us what the word means to you, and what it does not mean.

questions.label: Where should development begin, and why?
questions.hint: Start from a place, a group of people, a problem, or an idea — and explain your reasoning.

questions.label: What really matters about education?
questions.hint: What is education actually for? What does it do that nothing else does — and where does formal schooling fall short?

questions.label: Why do you want to join CTaDI, and what do you hope to contribute?
questions.hint: Be specific about what you would bring and what you would want to work on. "To learn and network" is not enough.

section_b.title: Section B — Your craft
section_b.subtitle: Only the questions for the role you selected. Concrete examples beat adjectives.

software_data.label: Software & Data
software_data.expectation: We expect working competence in at least one language and a data stack, and the judgement to know when software is not the answer.

questions.label: Which languages, frameworks and data tools do you actually use day to day, and what do you reach for them for?
questions.hint: Name them and say what each is good at. It is fine to say a tool is not your strength.

questions.label: Walk us through a project you are proud of: the problem, what you built, and what you would do differently now.
questions.hint: A link or repo is welcome, but the reasoning matters more than the link.

questions.label: Describe a time you chose NOT to build software — or chose the simplest possible solution. What did you weigh up?
questions.hint: We care about restraint and judgement as much as capability.

questions.label: How do you handle data that belongs to people — privacy, consent, ownership, and the possibility of harm?
questions.hint: Give a concrete situation you have faced or thought hard about.

questions.label: Rate your overall software/data proficiency from 1 to 5, and justify the number with one specific piece of evidence.
questions.hint: 1 = beginner, 3 = competent and independent, 5 = you would teach it. Your justification is scored, not your number.

hardware_energy.label: Hardware & Energy
hardware_energy.expectation: We expect hands-on ability with physical systems and an honest sense of what works in constrained, real-world conditions.

questions.label: What hardware, power or energy systems have you built, repaired, installed or measured yourself?
questions.hint: Bench work, field work, or coursework — say what you actually touched.

questions.label: Describe a project you are proud of: the constraints you worked under, what you achieved, and what failed.
questions.hint: Budget, climate, unreliable supply chains and maintenance realities all count as constraints.

questions.label: What breaks first in a real deployment, and how do you design for maintenance, repair and local ownership?
questions.hint: Think about what happens after the installers leave.

questions.label: How do you judge whether a technology is genuinely appropriate for a community — and what makes you say no to one?
questions.hint: Give an example of a technology you think is inappropriate, and why.

questions.label: Rate your overall hardware/energy proficiency from 1 to 5, and justify the number with one specific piece of evidence.
questions.hint: 1 = beginner, 3 = competent and independent, 5 = you would teach it. Your justification is scored, not your number.

policy_advocacy.label: Policy & Advocacy
policy_advocacy.expectation: We expect the ability to read a system, identify who holds power, and argue a case in writing and in person.

questions.label: Describe a policy, regulation or institutional decision you have engaged with — analysed, campaigned on, drafted or resisted.
questions.hint: Tell us what was at stake and what you actually did.

questions.label: Who holds power over the change you care about, and what would realistically move them?
questions.hint: Name the actors and the leverage, not just the ideal outcome.

questions.label: Describe a time you had to argue a case to someone who disagreed strongly. What did you do, and how did it go?
questions.hint: Failure stories are welcome if you learned something.

questions.label: How do you keep advocacy honest — avoiding both techno-optimism and doomerism, and staying accountable to affected communities?
questions.hint: Give a concrete example or a principle you have had to test.

questions.label: Rate your overall policy/advocacy proficiency from 1 to 5, and justify the number with one specific piece of evidence.
questions.hint: 1 = beginner, 3 = competent and independent, 5 = you would teach it. Your justification is scored, not your number.

design.label: Design
design.expectation: We expect design that starts from real users in real conditions, not from a mood board.

questions.label: Walk us through a design project you are proud of: who it was for, what you learned from them, and what you changed as a result.
questions.hint: Show the reasoning behind the decisions, not just the output.

questions.label: How do you design for people and contexts very different from your own — low bandwidth, low literacy, shared devices, limited power?
questions.hint: Concrete constraints, concrete decisions.

questions.label: What does accessibility and inclusion mean in your practice, beyond a checklist?
questions.hint: Give an example where it changed what you made.

questions.label: How do you tell whether your design actually helped? What evidence would change your mind?
questions.hint: We are interested in how you test reality, not how you defend your work.

questions.label: Rate your overall design proficiency from 1 to 5, and justify the number with one specific piece of evidence.
questions.hint: 1 = beginner, 3 = competent and independent, 5 = you would teach it. Your justification is scored, not your number.

research.label: Research
research.expectation: We expect the ability to form a real question, gather evidence honestly, and admit what the evidence does not show.

questions.label: Describe a piece of research you have done — formal or self-directed: the question, your method, and what you found.
questions.hint: A paper, report, thesis or a serious personal investigation all count.

questions.label: What is a question in your field that you think is badly asked, and how would you ask it better?
questions.hint: This is about judgement and framing, not about knowing the literature perfectly.

questions.label: How do you work with people as participants rather than as subjects — consent, benefit, and returning what you learn?
questions.hint: Give an example of how you put this into practice.

questions.label: Tell us about evidence that contradicted your expectations. What did you do with it?
questions.hint: We are looking for intellectual honesty, not a clean narrative.

questions.label: Rate your overall research proficiency from 1 to 5, and justify the number with one specific piece of evidence.
questions.hint: 1 = beginner, 3 = competent and independent, 5 = you would teach it. Your justification is scored, not your number.

operations.label: Operations
operations.expectation: We expect the ability to make things actually happen: logistics, budgets, people, and the unglamorous follow-through.

questions.label: Describe an operation, event, programme or process you ran end to end. What was your part, and what did it take to make it work?
questions.hint: Scale does not matter. Reliability does.

questions.label: How do you plan when money, time and people are all tight? Walk us through a real trade-off you made.
questions.hint: Tell us what you cut, and why.

questions.label: How do you keep a distributed or volunteer team coordinated, accountable and motivated without burning them out?
questions.hint: Give an example of a system or habit you put in place.

questions.label: What does good record-keeping and handover look like to you, and why does it matter for an organisation like CTaDI?
questions.hint: Think about what happens when one person leaves.

questions.label: Rate your overall operations proficiency from 1 to 5, and justify the number with one specific piece of evidence.
questions.hint: 1 = beginner, 3 = competent and independent, 5 = you would teach it. Your justification is scored, not your number.

questions.label: Realistically, how many hours per week can you commit to CTaDI over the next six months, and how does that fit alongside your other work or study?
questions.hint: A modest, honest answer is better than an ambitious one you cannot keep.

questions.label: How would you like to be involved — a specific project, ongoing volunteering, occasional advice, or something else?
questions.hint: Tell us what you would want to start with.
